figures.caption: FIG. 2. Structural transition probed by AFM and XRD | a Doubly differentiated AFM image (effectively mapping the surface normal) under ambient conditions where surface inclination direction and amplitude are colourcoded as indicated in b. Four domain types are present as expected from Fig. 1c, labelled I–IV. b Inclination directions (I–IV) extracted from the AFM scan, with the corresponding rhombohedral distortions shown exaggerated in c. d 3D-XRD measurement projected onto the Q[100]–Q[010] plane (in-plane directions), showing four peaks consistent with the four domain types identified by AFM. e Doubly differentiated AFM scan at the same position as a under applied stress of 0.7 GPa. Domains I and III vanish with increasing strain while domains II and IV extend over the entire scan area. f Under strain, the inclinations of the two remaining domain types (denoted as α and β ) are oriented along the [001] axis, as expected of two orthorhombic domains g. h 3D-XRD projection under maximal strain; the four peaks merge into two, as well as the emergence of a third peak (indicated with a black ’+’ right above the main peak).

FIG. 5. Domain relaxation captured by repeated AFM error signal measurements at different times. a Fit of the exponential decay of the domain activity after the external stress is released. b Measurement directly after the external stress is released. e Almost seven hours afterwards with intermediate measurements (c, d). Spike domains are still retracting from the upper part of the scan area towards the lower part under zero external stress. Selected spike domains retracting in (b-c) highlighted by black arrows and similarly for (d-e) indicated by red arrows.

FIG. 4. Strain-dependent phonon behaviour of LAO | a Three major modes in LAO corresponding to two Eg modes and one A1g mode energetically between them. b Typical Raman spectrum of LAO (001) under ambient conditions showing three peaks. c Strain-dependent Raman spectra in the vicinity of the most intense Eg mode displaying a strain-induced lifting of degeneracy (data fitted with a pair of Voigt profiles in black). d Eg peak splitting and A1g peak softening as a function of strain, extracted from peak fits and extracted values linearly fitted (black). e First-principles phonon dispersion of unstrained LAO near the Γ-point. f Phonon dispersion under 0.1% strain, showing lifting of Eg degeneracy at the Γ-point. g Modal behaviour of calculations performed across several strain levels between 0% and 0.1% confirming the behaviours for both the Eg splitting and the A1g mode softening, as indicated by linear fits (black).

FIG. 6. Strain cycling and relaxation qualified by the AFM error signal (a-d) and XRD intensity (e-h). a AFM measurement of the initial unstrained sample with four domain types. b Sample at maximum strain with two faintly visible domain types α and β . c Destrained sample after several strain cycles with four types of domains, but compared to a with additional spike domains. d Unstrained sample after 6.67 h of relaxation. Almost all of the additional domains disappeared from the scanned area. e-h XRD measurement of an entirely relaxed, unstrained sample, under maximal strain, imediately at the point of zero applied strain, and after 14 hours of relaxation. Note the projection here includes vertical peak splitting due to the Kα doublet, unlike the in-plane projection in the main text. Each reciprocal space map is analogue to the AFM image above it.

FIG. 3. In-plane twin wall angle rotation | a Full strain cycle applying (a1–a4) and releasing (a5–a8) compressive strain, along the horizontal axis, up to 0.48% (∼0.7 GPa stress) captured by AFM error signal scans (scale-bar 10 µm). a1 Domain walls form zig-zag lines inclined at 45◦ as expected from Fig. 1c. With increasing strain the angle decreases continuously until the walls flatten to 0◦ (a4), accompanied by one domain type progressively consuming the surface area of the other. a5–a8 The process is fully reversible: upon strain release the domain wall angle increases and the surface share of the receding domain type recovers. b In-plane domain wall angle with resprect to the (010) plane as a function of applied strain, extracted from the dashed region in a1–a4, analysed independently for the two domain wall orientations (yellow and green), a line (black) is a guide to the eye. The domain wall angle evolves continuously with strain.

FIG. 1. LAO lattice structure, domain formation and strain response. | a Pseudo-cubic LAO lattice with oxygen octahedra (red) slightly rotated about the [111] axis. b Four symmetry-allowed domain orientations on the (001) surface with characteristic strain distortions. c Chevron twin pattern on the (001) LAO surface (transparent green surface in a) comprising four domain types separated by walls along the [010] and [110] directions. d Schematic of the homebuilt piezo-driven strain cell. e (50×50) µm2 AFM height scan revealing ferroelastic microdomains (with a few micrometer periodicity) superimposed by non-ferroelastic structures (few tens of micrometer periodicity). f Vertically averaged line scans (white dashed region in e) showing inclined surface normals forming a stepped structure. g AFM scan under 0.48% applied compressive strain (strain axis indicated by grey arrows) showing a strongly reduced surface substructure. h AFM height line scan under strain demonstrating surface flattening relative to f.
